claim: Coliphage HK022 Nun blocks superinfection by coliphage λ by stalling RNA polymerase (RNAP) translocation specifically on λ DNA.
source: Coliphage HK022 Nun blocks superinfection by coliphage λ by stalling RNA polymerase (RNAP) translocation specifically on λ DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Robert et al., 1987; Hung and Gottesman, 1997; Vitiello et al., 2014) as indicated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Structures of Escherichia coli RNAP ternary elongation complexes (TECs) with and without Nun were determined by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
source: To provide a structural framework to understand how Nun blocks RNAP translocation, we determined structures of Escherichia coli RNAP ternary elongation complexes (TECs) with and without Nun by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used to determine the structures.

claim: Nun fits tightly into the TEC by taking advantage of gaps between the RNAP and the nucleic acids.
source: Nun fits tightly into the TEC by taking advantage of gaps between the RNAP and the nucleic acids.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminal segment of Nun interacts with the RNAP β and β' subunits inside the RNAP active site cleft as well as with nearly every element of the nucleic acid scaffold.
source: The C-terminal segment of Nun interacts with the RNAP β and β' subunits inside the RNAP active site cleft as well as with nearly every element of the nucleic acid scaffold, essentially crosslinking the RNAP and the nucleic acids to prevent translocation, a mechanism supported by the effects of Nun amino acid substitutions.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and mutagenesis experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Nun essentially crosslinks the RNAP and the nucleic acids to prevent translocation.
source: The C-terminal segment of Nun interacts with the RNAP β and β' subunits inside the RNAP active site cleft as well as with nearly every element of the nucleic acid scaffold, essentially crosslinking the RNAP and the nucleic acids to prevent translocation, a mechanism supported by the effects of Nun amino acid substitutions.
evidence: This mechanism is inferred from the structural data and supported by mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The nature of Nun interactions inside the RNAP active site cleft suggests that RNAP clamp opening is required for Nun to establish its interactions.
source: The nature of Nun interactions inside the RNAP active site cleft suggests that RNAP clamp opening is required for Nun to establish its interactions, explaining why Nun acts on paused TECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and knowledge of TEC pausing mechanisms.

claim: Nun acts on paused TECs because RNAP clamp opening is required for Nun to establish its interactions.
source: The nature of Nun interactions inside the RNAP active site cleft suggests that RNAP clamp opening is required for Nun to establish its interactions, explaining why Nun acts on paused TECs.
evidence: This explanation is based on structural inference and knowledge of pausing mechanisms.

claim: The 13 kDa Nun protein of coliphage HK022 has one known function, to exclude superinfection by the rival coliphage λ.
source: The 13 kDa Nun protein of coliphage HK022 has one known function, to exclude superinfection by the rival coliphage λ (Robert et al., 1987) by arresting host Escherichia coli (Eco) RNAP transcription specifically on λ DNA (Hung and Gottesman, 1997; Vitiello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nun arrests host Escherichia coli RNAP transcription specifically on λ DNA.
source: The 13 kDa Nun protein of coliphage HK022 has one known function, to exclude superinfection by the rival coliphage λ (Robert et al., 1987) by arresting host Escherichia coli (Eco) RNAP transcription specifically on λ DNA (Hung and Gottesman, 1997; Vitiello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HK022 Nun competes with, and antagonizes the function of, the λ N antitermination protein.
source: HK022 Nun competes with, and antagonizes the function of, the λ N antitermination protein (Robert et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun achieves specificity by binding to the cis-acting boxB RNA hairpin within nut (N-utilization) RNA sequences in λ nascent transcripts through an N-terminal arginine-rich motif, or ARM.
source: Like λ N, Nun achieves specificity by binding to the cis-acting boxB RNA hairpin within nut (N-utilization) RNA sequences in λ nascent transcripts through an N-terminal arginine-rich motif, or ARM (Chattopadhyay et al., 1995; Faber et al., 2001; Schärpf et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Unlike λ N, which suppresses transcription termination at terminators downstream of the nut sites, Nun provokes premature downstream termination.
source: Unlike λ N, which suppresses transcription termination at terminators downstream of the nut sites, Nun provokes premature downstream termination (Robert et al., 1987; Robledo et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: After localization to specific ternary elongation complexes (TECs) containing the λ nut sequence, the C-terminal segment of Nun interacts with the TEC to block RNAP translocation (forward or reverse) at intrinsic pause sites without affecting RNAP catalytic activity and without dissociating the complex.
source: After localization to specific ternary elongation complexes (TECs) containing the λ nut sequence, the C-terminal segment of Nun interacts with the TEC to block RNAP translocation (forward or reverse) at intrinsic pause sites without affecting RNAP catalytic activity and without dissociating the complex (Hung and Gottesman, 1997; Vitiello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nun-mediated transcription termination in vivo depends on the function of the Mfd protein, which can remove the arrested TECs from the DNA template.
source: Nun-mediated transcription termination in vivo depends on the function of the Mfd protein, which can remove the arrested TECs from the DNA template (Washburn et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: At normal in vivo expression levels, Nun acts only on TECs containing the λ nut sequence, and Nun function is dependent on NusA, NusB, NusE, and NusG.
source: At normal in vivo expression levels, Nun acts only on TECs containing the λ nut sequence, and Nun function is dependent on NusA, NusB, NusE, and NusG (Robert et al., 1987; Robledo et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At high expression levels in vivo, Nun is toxic to Eco cells as it acts to arrest transcription elongation by the host RNAP nonspecifically.
source: At high expression levels in vivo, Nun is toxic to Eco cells as it acts to arrest transcription elongation by the host RNAP nonspecifically (Uc-Mass et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun alone arrests Eco TECs without λ N nut RNA elements and independent of Nus factors when present at high concentration in vitro.
source: Nun alone arrests Eco TECs without λ N nut RNA elements and independent of Nus factors when present at high concentration in vitro (Hung and Gottesman, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The X-Nun/TEC-20A structure was determined to 3.7 Å resolution.
source: We present three cryoEM reconstructions, glutaraldehyde crosslinked Nun/TEC-20A (X-Nun/TEC-20A; 3.7 Å overall resolution; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a direct report of the resolution achieved in the cryoEM reconstruction.

claim: The X-TEC-20A structure was determined to 4.1 Å resolution.
source: glutaraldehyde crosslinked TEC-20A (X-TEC-20A; 4.1 Å overall resolution; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a direct report of the resolution achieved in the cryoEM reconstruction.

claim: The TEC-20A structure was determined to 4.4 Å resolution.
source: TEC-20A without glutaraldehyde crosslinking (4.4 Å overall resolution; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the resolution achieved in the cryoEM reconstruction.

claim: Superposition of all three structures by RNAP Cα positions resulted in root mean square deviations of <0.7 Å over at least 2750 Cα's.
source: Superposition of all three structures by RNAP Cα positions resulted in root mean square deviations of <0.7 Å over at least 2750 Cα's (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from structural comparison.

claim: The crosslinking did not trap rare conformations.
source: From the structural correspondence between TEC-20A and X-TEC-20A, we conclude that the crosslinked structures are representative of the uncrosslinked solution structures (i.e. the crosslinking did not trap rare conformations; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural comparison data.

claim: The TEC accommodates Nun without global conformational changes.
source: From the structural correspondence between TEC-20A, X-TEC-20A, and X-Nun/TEC-20A, we conclude that the TEC accommodates Nun without global conformational changes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural comparison data.

claim: Much of the central core of the X-Nun/TEC-20A structure, including the active site, the 9 bp RNA/DNA hybrid, and much of the visible part of Nun, was determined to 3.3–3.6 Å resolution.
source: The overall resolution of the X-Nun/TEC-20A cryoEM density map was 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F) but local resolution calculations indicate much of the central core of the structure, including the active site, the 9 bp RNA/DNA hybrid, and much of the visible part of Nun, was determined to 3.3–3.6 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is based on local resolution calculations from the cryoEM data.

claim: In TEC-20A, the downstream duplex DNA enters the active site cleft and begins unwinding at +1.
source: In TEC-20A, the downstream duplex DNA enters the active site cleft and begins unwinding at +1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The nt-strand G at +1 binds in a G-specific pocket of the β-subunit.
source: The nt-strand G at +1 binds in a G-specific pocket of the β-subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as observed in initiation complex structures (Bae et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure and is consistent with prior structural studies.

claim: A G at the +1 position of the na-scaffold facilitates Nun-mediated translocation arrest.
source: A G at this position of the na-scaffold facilitates Nun-mediated translocation arrest (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 9-bp RNA/DNA hybrid is in the post-translocated state, with the 3'-end of the RNA at −1.
source: The 9-bp RNA/DNA hybrid is in the post-translocated state, with the 3'-end of the RNA at −1 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The β'lid directly blocks the upstream extension of the RNA/DNA hybrid.
source: The β'lid directly blocks the upstream extension of the RNA/DNA hybrid (Bernecky et al., 2016; Vassylyev et al., 2007; Westover et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with prior studies.

claim: Conserved hydrophobic residues V253 and L255 interact with the face of the last upstream RNA/DNA bp at −9, possibly providing a 'greasy' surface for the bases to slip past during translocation.
source: Conserved hydrophobic residues V253 and L255 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) interact with the face of the last upstream RNA/DNA bp at −9, possibly providing a 'greasy' surface for the bases to slip past during translocation.
evidence: This is a structural observation with a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: V253 appears to help track the upstream ssRNA towards the RNA exit channel.
source: V253 appears to help track the upstream ssRNA towards the RNA exit channel (to the left of the β'lid in Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural position of V253.

claim: Conserved R259 of the β'lid directs the t-strand DNA away from the RNA.
source: Conserved R259 of theβ'lid (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) directs the t-strand DNA away from the RNA (to the right of the β'lid in Figure 3)
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Conserved D256, at the top of the β'lid, forms a salt bridge with conserved R841 descending from the βflap.
source: Conserved D256 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), at the top of the β'lid, forms a salt bridge with conserved R841 descending from the βflap, which covers the top of the RNA exit channel (Figures 2A and 3).
evidence: This is a structural observation of a specific interaction.

claim: Interactions between the βflap and elements of the β' subunit seal off the nucleic acid tracks, preventing the upstream ssRNA and t-strand DNA from slipping over the top of the β'lid and inappropriately displacing the nt-strand DNA to form an extended RNA/DNA hybrid.
source: This and other interactions between the βflap and elements of the β' subunit seal off the nucleic acid tracks, preventing the upstream ssRNA and t-strand DNA from slipping over the top of the β'lid and inappropriately displacing the nt-strand DNA to form an extended RNA/DNA hybrid (Naryshkina et al., 2006; Toulokhonov and Landick, 2006).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of structural observations, supported by prior work.

claim: The -10 t-strand nucleotide base pairs with the nt-strand DNA to begin the upstream DNA duplex with no single-stranded gap in the t-strand DNA.
source: The -10 t-strand nucleotide base pairs with the nt-strand DNA to begin the upstream DNA duplex with no single-stranded gap in the t-strand DNA (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: Density for the upstream DNA duplex is weak and noisy, indicative of mobility.
source: Density for the upstream DNA duplex is weak and noisy, indicative of mobility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quality of the cryoEM density.

claim: The -10 bp is distorted.
source: The density maps and refinement results indicate that the -10 bp is distorted (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), consistent with the conclusions of (Turtola and Belogurov, 2016).
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with prior work.

claim: Conserved R47 of the β'zipper interacts with the nt-strand -12 backbone phosphate, helping to set the path of the upstream DNA duplex.
source: Upstream of the β'lid, conserved R47 of the β'zipper (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) interacts with the nt-strand -12 backbone phosphate (Figure 3), helping to set the path of the upstream DNA duplex
evidence: This is a structural observation with a functional interpretation.

claim: The upstream DNA duplex exits the complex without any steric clashes, subtending an angle of about 110° with the entering downstream duplex DNA.
source: which exits the complex without any steric clashes, subtending an angle of about 110° with the entering downstream duplex DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: Only the C-terminal 23 residues (residues 87–109) of Nun were visible in the structure.
source: Although the X-Nun/TEC-20A complex contained full-length Nun (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), only the C-terminal 23 residues (residues 87–109), which contain all known determinants for the translocation arrest activity of Nun (Henthorn and Friedman, 1996; Kim and Gottesman, 2004; Watnick et al., 2000), were visible in the structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure, with citation to prior work on functional determinants.

claim: The C-terminal 23 residues of Nun contain all known determinants for the translocation arrest activity of Nun.
source: only the C-terminal 23 residues (residues 87–109), which contain all known determinants for the translocation arrest activity of Nun (Henthorn and Friedman, 1996; Kim and Gottesman, 2004; Watnick et al., 2000), were visible in the structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nun forms an extended structure that worms its way into the TEC active site cleft, interacting with the β'zipper, then squeezing through the nt-strand DNA track between the β'lid and the β'rudder, then between the β'rudder and the RNA/DNA hybrid.
source: Nun forms an extended structure that worms its way into the TEC active site cleft, interacting with the β'zipper, then squeezing through the nt-strand DNA track between the β'lid and the β'rudder, then between the β'rudder and the RNA/DNA hybrid.
evidence: This is a description of the structural path of Nun through the TEC.

claim: The very C-terminal segment of Nun (residues 102–109) binds in a pre-existing pocket next to the β'rudder between the downstream duplex DNA and the RNA/DNA hybrid.
source: The very C-terminal segment of Nun (residues 102–109) binds in a pre-existing pocket next to the β'rudder between the downstream duplex DNA and the RNA/DNA hybrid (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: Nun expands the narrow space between the β'lid, the β'rudder, and the beginning of the upstream duplex DNA by pushing the upstream DNA duplex outwards (away from the RNAP) about 3.5 Å, a full bp step.
source: The overall structure of the TEC is largely unchanged (Supplementary file 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B), but Nun expands the narrow space between the β'lid, the β'rudder, and the beginning of the upstream duplex DNA by pushing the upstream DNA duplex outwards (away from the RNAP) about 3.5 Å, a full bp step (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation.

claim: Nun residue H93 stacks on the exposed downstream face of the nt-strand DNA -10 base.
source: Nun residue H93 stacks on the exposed downstream face of the nt-strand DNA -10 base while R94 reaches to the major groove edge of the -10 bp, where it forms a hydrogen-bond (H-bond) with the O4 atom of the t-strand -10T (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation of a specific interaction from the structure.

claim: Nun R94 reaches to the major groove edge of the -10 bp, where it forms a hydrogen-bond with the O4 atom of the t-strand -10T.
source: Nun residue H93 stacks on the exposed downstream face of the nt-strand DNA -10 base while R94 reaches to the major groove edge of the -10 bp, where it forms a hydrogen-bond (H-bond) with the O4 atom of the t-strand -10T (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation of a specific interaction from the structure.

claim: The Nun R94 interaction with the -10 bp is not likely to be sequence-specific since Nun R94 has the reach and flexibility to form a H-bond with a H-acceptor on the major groove edge of either the nt-strand or t-strand base.
source: This interaction is not likely to be sequence-specific since Nun R94 has the reach and flexibility to form a H-bond with a H-acceptor on the major groove edge of either the nt-strand or t-strand base.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural flexibility and reach of R94.

claim: The presence of Nun in the vicinity of the upstream DNA duplex accounts for the Nun-dependent upstream toe-print.
source: The presence of Nun in the vicinity of the upstream DNA duplex accounts for the Nun-dependent upstream toe-print (Vitiello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observation to prior experimental data.

claim: Nun squeezes between the β'rudder and the RNA/DNA hybrid, displacing some α-carbons of the rudder about 3 Å and altering some rudder/nucleic acid interactions.
source: Nun then squeezes between the β'rudder and the RNA/DNA hybrid (Figure 4C), displacing some α-carbons of the rudder about 3 Å and altering some rudder/nucleic acid interactions.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation.

claim: In the TEC, β'R322 of the rudder makes polar interactions with the -6 and -7 RNA nucleotides.
source: In particular, in the TEC, β'R322 of the rudder makes polar interactions with the -6 and -7 RNA nucleotides, but in the Nun/TEC complex, β'R322 is displaced and forms an Arg-His pair with Nun H98 (Heyda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a structural observation comparing TEC and Nun/TEC structures.

claim: In the Nun/TEC complex, β'R322 is displaced and forms an Arg-His pair with Nun H98.
source: In particular, in the TEC, β'R322 of the rudder makes polar interactions with the -6 and -7 RNA nucleotides, but in the Nun/TEC complex, β'R322 is displaced and forms an Arg-His pair with Nun H98 (Heyda et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a structural observation with citation to prior work on Arg-His pairs.

claim: Nun H98 forms H-bonds with the 2'-OH of the -7 and -8 RNA nucleotides.
source: Nun H98 in turn forms H-bonds with the 2'-OH of the -7 and -8 RNA nucleotides (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct observation of specific interactions from the structure.

claim: Replacing the RNA -7A with deoxy-A significantly reduced the transcription arrest efficiency of Nun.
source: We tested the validity of this observation by replacing the RNA -7A with deoxy-A (so disrupting the Nun H98/-7 RNA 2'-OH interaction), which did not affect elongation in the absence of Nun in the C10 extension assay, but significantly reduced the transcription arrest efficiency of Nun (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data testing the functional importance of the observed interaction.

claim: The new position of β'R322 is stabilized by a salt bridge with β'D264 at the base of the lid.
source: The new position of β'R322 is stabilized by a salt bridge with β'D264 at the base of the lid.
evidence: This is a structural observation of a specific interaction.

claim: Substitutions β'R322H or β'D264G lead to Nun resistance in vivo.
source: This configuration is important since substitutions β'R322H or β'D264G lead to Nun resistance in vivo (Robledo et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun residues N97 and H100 complete a network of polar interactions with the RNA, the t-strand DNA, and the β'rudder.
source: Along with H98, nearby Nun residues N97 and H100 complete a network of polar interactions with the RNA, the t-strand DNA, and the β'rudder (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation of multiple interactions.

claim: The negatively-charged C-terminal carboxylate of Nun (S109) forms a salt bridge with Nun R102, resulting in an 8-residue non-covalent circle.
source: The negatively-charged C-terminal carboxylate of Nun (S109) forms a salt bridge with Nun R102, resulting in an 8-residue non-covalent circle (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct observation of a specific intramolecular interaction from the structure.

claim: The substitution Nun R102A significantly reduced termination efficiency.
source: The substitution Nun R102A significantly reduced termination efficiency (Kim and Gottesman, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun residues from N101 to the C-terminus form a network of polar interactions with the β-subunit, the RNA (-6), the downstream duplex DNA (+4t, +5t), and the nt-strand ssDNA (-1nt).
source: Nun residues from N101 to the C-terminus form a network of polar interactions with the β-subunit, the RNA (-6), the downstream duplex DNA (+4t, +5t), and the nt-strand ssDNA (-1nt) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation of multiple interactions.

claim: The interaction between Nun N105 and the nt-strand ssDNA (-1nt) explains why a two nucleotide nt-strand non-complementary 5'-overhang at the downstream fork of the transcription bubble is necessary for optimal Nun function.
source: The latter interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) explains why a two nucleotide nt-strand non-complementary 5'-overhang at the downstream fork of the transcription bubble is necessary for optimal Nun function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting a structural observation to experimental data.

claim: The substitution β'D329G leads to Nun resistance.
source: In addition to RNAP substitutions β'R322H and D264G, the substitution β'D329G leads to Nun resistance (Robledo et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: β'D329 forms part of a pocket in the RNAP structure that accommodates Nun W108.
source: β'D329 forms part of a pocket in the RNAP structure that accommodates Nun W108 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The structure is consistent with previous findings that the C-terminus of Nun is within 15–20 Å of the downstream duplex DNA.
source: The structure is consistent with previous findings that the C-terminus of Nun is within 15–20 Å of the downstream duplex DNA (Watnick and Gottesman, 1999).
evidence: This is a comparison of the structure with prior experimental data.

claim: Normal Nun activity required an aromatic residue at Nun position 108.
source: The location of the Nun C-terminus within the vicinity of the downstream duplex DNA, combined with the finding that normal Nun activity required an aromatic residue at Nun position 108 led to the proposal that Nun-mediated translocation arrest was facilitated by the intercalation of Nun W108 into the downstream DNA (Watnick and Gottesman, 1999) but this is not observed in the structure.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun W108 does not intercalate into the downstream DNA.
source: The location of the Nun C-terminus within the vicinity of the downstream duplex DNA, combined with the finding that normal Nun activity required an aromatic residue at Nun position 108 led to the proposal that Nun-mediated translocation arrest was facilitated by the intercalation of Nun W108 into the downstream DNA (Watnick and Gottesman, 1999) but this is not observed in the structure.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure that contradicts a prior hypothesis.

claim: A segment of Nun encompassing residues 44 to the C-terminus (residue 109) was found to crosslink to both the 5'- and 3'-ends of RNA transcripts.
source: A segment of Nun encompassing residues 44 to the C-terminus (residue 109) was found to crosslink to both the 5'- and 3'-ends of RNA transcripts (Mustaev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nun 44-109 crosslinks to the RNA 5'-end when the crosslinking moiety is placed at the -9 to -14 positions.
source: Nun 44-109 crosslinks to the RNA 5'-end when the crosslinking moiety is placed at the -9 to -14 positions.
evidence: This is a description of prior experimental results.

claim: Nun residues 44–86 exit the TEC near the RNA exit channel and could easily reach the upstream RNA, assuming some breathing/opening of the RNA exit channel.
source: These positions would not be able to crosslink to the Nun C-terminus (residues 87-109) visible in our structure, but Nun residues 44–86 exit the TEC near the RNA exit channel (Figure 1C) and could easily reach the upstream RNA, assuming some breathing/opening of the RNA exit channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure and prior crosslinking data.

claim: Nun crosslinks to the RNA 3'-end in a 2-nucleotide backtracked complex.
source: Nun crosslinks to the RNA 3-'end in a 2-nucleotide backtracked complex (Mustaev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Structures of both bacterial and eukaryotic TECs backtracked by 1-nucleotide place the backtracked nucleotide (+2 position) in the so-called 'P'-site.
source: Structures of both bacterial and eukaryotic TECs backtracked by 1-nucleotide place the backtracked nucleotide (+2 position) in the so-called 'P'-site (Sekine et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural work.

claim: A eukaryotic 2-nucleotide backtracked complex shows the first backtracked nucleotide (+2) again in the P-site, while the second (3') backtracked nucleotide (+3) is disordered.
source: A eukaryotic 2-nucleotide backtracked complex shows the first backtracked nucleotide (+2) again in the P-site, while the second (3') backtracked nucleotide (+3) is disordered, consistent with molecular dynamics simulations showing the +3 nucleotide sampling a large range of conformations (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural and computational work.

claim: The closest atom of Nun to the RNAP active site Mg2+ is 27 Å away.
source: Thus, although the closest atom of Nun to the RNAP active site Mg2+ is 27 Å away, the flexible nature of the 2-nucleotide backtracked complex would allow the crosslinking moiety on the base of the RNA 3'-nucleotide to reach Nun.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structure.

claim: The flexible nature of the 2-nucleotide backtracked complex would allow the crosslinking moiety on the base of the RNA 3'-nucleotide to reach Nun.
source: Thus, although the closest atom of Nun to the RNAP active site Mg2+ is 27 Å away, the flexible nature of the 2-nucleotide backtracked complex would allow the crosslinking moiety on the base of the RNA 3'-nucleotide to reach Nun.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure and knowledge of backtracked complex flexibility.

claim: Nun mutants H93A, R94A, N97D, H98A, H100A, R102A, R102K, K106A, K107A, K106A/K107A, and W108A were generated and tested for activity in vitro.
source: Based on our structural analyses, we generated single (and one double) amino acid substitutions in Nun and tested their activity in vitro. We substituted residues that appeared to make important interactions, including H93A and R94A (Figure 4B), N97D, H98A, and H100A (Figure 4C), and R102A, R102K, K106A, K107A, K106A/K107A, and W108A (Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to test the structural observations.

claim: Nun N103 does not appear to make important interactions in the structure.
source: Nun N103 does not appear to make important interactions in the structure (Figure 4A), so the N103A substitution served as a control.
evidence: This is a structural observation used to justify the choice of a control mutation.

claim: The Nun mutants displayed a wide range of activities, from 21 ± 7(SEM)% for H98A to 96 ± 4% for N103A.
source: The Nun mutants displayed a wide range of activities (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), from 21 ± 7(SEM)% for H98A to 96 ± 4% for N103A (essentially wild-type, consistent with our structural analysis).
evidence: This is experimental data from the mutagenesis study.

claim: The binding and activity of the Nun mutants are not strictly correlated.
source: The binding and activity of the Nun mutants are not strictly correlated (Figure 5B), indicating that some substitutions have a strong effect on binding but not on activity (R94A), while others affect binding to a lesser degree but have a stronger effect on activity (H98A).
evidence: This is an analysis of the experimental data from the mutagenesis study.

claim: Each of the tested Nun mutants show significant translocation arrest activity (59% to 80% of wt-Nun) when assayed at saturating concentration despite widely varying effects on RNAP binding.
source: Nevertheless, each of the tested mutants show significant translocation arrest activity (59% to 80% of wt-Nun) when assayed at saturating concentration despite widely varying effects on RNAP binding (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data from the mutagenesis study.

claim: Efficient transcription elongation requires that the na-scaffold slide freely with respect to the RNAP at each step of translocation in a nucleic acid sequence-independent manner.
source: Efficient transcription elongation requires that the na-scaffold slide freely with respect to the RNAP at each step of translocation in a nucleic acid sequence-independent manner.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of transcription elongation.

claim: The RNAP does not form tight, cognate interactions with most of the na-scaffold in the TEC.
source: As a consequence, the RNAP does not form tight, cognate interactions with most of the na-scaffold in the TEC (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural requirements for translocation.

claim: Nun establishes its interactions with the TEC by taking advantage of the loose RNAP/na-scaffold interactions, insinuating itself into the TEC in pre-existing gaps between the RNAP and the upstream duplex DNA, the t-strand DNA connecting the upstream duplex DNA with the RNA/DNA hybrid, and in a pocket next to the rudder between the RNA/DNA hybrid and the downstream duplex DNA.
source: Nun establishes its interactions with the TEC by taking advantage of the loose RNAP/na-scaffold interactions, insinuating itself into the TEC in pre-existing gaps between the RNAP and the upstream duplex DNA (Figure 6A), the t-strand DNA connecting the upstream duplex DNA with the RNA/DNA hybrid (Figure 6B), and in a pocket next to the rudder between the RNA/DNA hybrid and the downstream duplex DNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a summary of structural observations.

claim: The Nun/TEC interactions induce some small, localized conformational changes but do not cause large-scale changes in the TEC.
source: The Nun/TEC interactions induce some small, localized conformational changes (such as in the upstream duplex, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, or in the rudder, Figures 2 and 6C), but do not cause large-scale changes in the TEC (Supplementary file 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a summary of structural comparison data.

claim: Nun interacts with nearly every element of the na-scaffold: the upstream duplex DNA, the RNA/DNA hybrid, the single-stranded nt-strand DNA within the transcription bubble, and the downstream duplex DNA.
source: At the same time, Nun interacts with nearly every element of the na-scaffold: the upstream duplex DNA, the RNA/DNA hybrid, the single-stranded nt-strand DNA within the transcription bubble, and the downstream duplex DNA (Figures 4 and 7).
evidence: This is a summary of structural observations.

claim: With this network of Nun/RNAP and Nun/na-scaffold interactions, Nun essentially mediates extensive crosslinking between the RNAP and the na-scaffold, preventing sliding of the na-scaffold with respect to the RNAP (i.e. preventing translocation).
source: With this network of Nun/RNAP and Nun/na-scaffold interactions, Nun essentially mediates extensive crosslinking between the RNAP and the na-scaffold, preventing sliding of the na-scaffold with respect to the RNAP (i.e. preventing translocation).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the structural observations.

claim: This mechanism explains how Nun arrests both forward and reverse translocation.
source: Note that this mechanism explains how Nun arrests both forward and reverse translocation (Vitiello et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural mechanism to prior experimental observations.

claim: The finding that Nun establishes multiple interactions with both the RNAP and na-scaffold explains how single amino acid substitutions in Nun still retain significant translocation arrest function.
source: The finding that Nun establishes multiple interactions with both the RNAP and na-scaffold explains how single amino acid substitutions in Nun still retain significant translocation arrest function (Figure 5) since the disruption of one or a few interactions still leaves many other interactions that the TEC must overcome in order to translocate (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observations to the mutagenesis data.

claim: Nun does not contain a functional center of critical amino acids for its translocation arrest activity; all of the Nun/TEC interactions contribute to its function.
source: Nun does not contain a functional center of critical amino acids for its translocation arrest activity; all of the Nun/TEC interactions contribute to its function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: In phage HK022 lysogens, the concentration of Nun in the Eco cell is likely to be only ~100 nM.
source: In phage HK022 lysogens, the concentration of Nun ([Nun]) in the Eco cell is likely to be only ~100 nM (King et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Kd of wt-Nun for a non-specific TEC is ~300 nM.
source: The Kd of wt-Nun for a non-specific TEC (i.e. not containing λ nut boxB RNA) is ~300 nM (Figure 5)
evidence: This is experimental data from the binding studies.

claim: The Kd for a TEC containing a boxB RNA hairpin would be expected to be lower than for a non-specific TEC.
source: while the Kd for a TEC containing a boxB RNA hairpin would be expected to be lower.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known boxB-binding function of Nun.

claim: Nun function is stimulated in vivo and in vitro by NusA, NusB, NusE, and NusG, but only in the presence of λ nut boxA RNA.
source: Nun function is stimulated in vivo and in vitro by NusA, NusB, NusE, and NusG, but only in the presence of λ nut boxA RNA (Hung and Gottesman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Nus factors likely stabilize Nun binding to λ nut TECs.
source: The mechanism of Nus factor stimulation of Nun activity is unknown, but the Nus factors likely stabilize Nun binding to λ nut TECs.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of Nus factor stimulation.

claim: The concentration of Nun in phage HK022 lysogens is precisely tuned to allow Nun to target λ nut TECs but not cause general translocation arrest throughout the Eco genome.
source: These observations indicate that [Nun] in phage HK022 lysogens is precisely tuned to allow Nun to target λ nut TECs but not cause general translocation arrest throughout the Eco genome (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data and knowledge of in vivo Nun concentrations.

claim: Nun mutants H98A, K106A/K107A, and W108A have been shown previously to be significantly (K106A/K107A) or totally (H98A, W108A) defective in Nun function both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Nun mutants H98A, K106A/K107A, and W108A have been shown previously to be significantly (K106A/K107A) or totally (H98A, W108A) defective in Nun function both in vivo and in vitro (Kim and Gottesman, 2004; Watnick and Gottesman, 1999; Watnick et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At saturating [Nun], the mutants H98A, W108A, and K106A/K107A exhibit significant translocation arrest activity (H98A, 59%; W108A, 66%; K106A/K107A, >70%).
source: These results appear to contradict our results that, at saturating [Nun], these mutants exhibit significant translocation arrest activity (H98A, 59%; W108A, 66%; K106A/K107A, >70%; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the current study.

claim: Previous studies assessed mutant Nun activity at [Nun] too low to overcome the binding defects introduced by the mutations.
source: However, in previous studies, In vivo function was assessed using a λ pL-nutL-lacZ chromosomal transcriptional fusion (Wilson et al., 1997) with very low expression levels of the Nun mutants. In vitro transcription reactions included between 50–200 nM Nun mutants. In our study, significant activity of the Nun mutants was observed at saturating [Nun] >250 µM (Figure 5). Thus, the previous studies assessed mutant Nun activity at [Nun] too low to overcome the binding defects introduced by the mutations.
evidence: This is an inference reconciling the current results with prior work.

claim: In the final state of the Nun/TEC complex, Nun forms extensive interactions with both the RNAP clamp domain, the na-scaffold, as well as with elements of the β subunit apposing the clamp, tightening and immobilizing normally mobile elements of the TEC.
source: In the final state of the Nun/TEC complex determined here (Figure 1C), Nun forms extensive interactions with both the RNAP clamp domain, the na-scaffold, as well as with elements of the β subunit apposing the clamp (Figure 7), tightening and immobilizing normally mobile elements of the TEC
evidence: This is a summary of structural observations.

claim: The tightening and immobilization of TEC elements by Nun suggests why the X-Nun/TEC structure was determined to higher resolution than either the X-TEC or the TEC structures.
source: tightening and immobilizing normally mobile elements of the TEC, suggesting why the X-Nun/TEC structure was determined to higher resolution than either the X-TEC or the TEC structures (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observations to the resolution differences.

claim: It would not be possible for Nun to establish itself in this binding mode with the clamp domain tightly closed; clamp opening appears to be required for Nun binding.
source: Nun fits tightly into the TEC without causing major conformational changes in the TEC by taking advantage of pre-existing gaps between the RNAP and the na-scaffold (Figure 6), but examination of the structure suggests that it would not be possible for Nun to establish itself in this binding mode with the clamp domain tightly closed; clamp opening appears to be required for Nun binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on examination of the structure.

claim: There is no clear consensus sequence for Nun-mediated translocation arrest.
source: There is no clear consensus sequence for Nun-mediated translocation arrest, consistent with the Nun/TEC structure.
evidence: This is an observation consistent with the structural data.

claim: Nun does not arrest translocation at random sites on the DNA; Nun preferentially stalls translocation at pre-existing intrinsic transcription pause sites.
source: Nevertheless, Nun does not arrest translocation at random sites on the DNA; Nun preferentially stalls translocation at pre-existing intrinsic transcription pause sites (Hung and Gottesman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Structural and functional analysis of paused transcription complexes suggests that pausing is linked with a propensity for clamp opening.
source: Structural (Weixlbaumer et al., 2013) and functional (Hein et al., 2014) analysis of paused transcription complexes suggests that pausing is linked with a propensity for clamp opening.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Clamp opening is likely required for Nun entry, providing an explanation for the action of Nun at intrinsic pause sites.
source: This provides an explanation for the action of Nun at intrinsic pause sites, since clamp opening is likely required for Nun entry.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural requirement for clamp opening to the preference for pause sites.

claim: TEC pausing provides Nun with a sufficiently long-lived stationary target to establish its extensive network of interactions, which is likely a slow process.
source: In addition to clamp opening, TEC pausing provides Nun with a sufficiently long-lived stationary target to establish its extensive network of interactions, which is likely a slow process (Hung and Gottesman, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference with citation to prior work.

claim: The Nun:TEC stoichiometry is 1:1.
source: Two major charge-state series corresponding to experimental masses of 383,971 ± 8 Da and 396,705 ± 6 Da were observed in the mass spectrum of Nun/TEC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The lower mass (384.0 kDa) matches the expected mass of the fully assembled TEC within the accuracy of the measurement (0.05%). Importantly, the difference between the two measured masses is 12,734 Da, which is close to the expected mass of Nun (12,732 Da), revealing that the 396.7-kDa assembly consists of TEC with one Nun bound.
evidence: This is experimental data from native mass spectrometry.

claim: Eco TECs assembled from purified Eco core RNAP and the na-scaffold with a 9-nt post-translocated RNA transcript (TEC-9A) were active in transcription elongation.
source: Eco TECs assembled from purified Eco core RNAP and the na-scaffold with a 9-nt post-translocated RNA transcript (TEC-9A, since the RNA is 9-nt in length and contains A at the 3'-end; Figure 1A , 9A RNA) were active in transcription elongation (Figure 1B, lane 2).
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating TEC activity.

claim: In the presence of a saturating concentration of Nun (20 µM), essentially 100% of the post-translocated 9A transcript was extended to 10C.
source: Under the same conditions in the presence of a saturating concentration of Nun (20 µM), essentially 100% of the post-translocated 9A transcript was extended to 10C as expected (Vitiello et al., 2014), since this reaction did not require RNAP translocation on the template (Figure 1B, compare lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating Nun does not inhibit catalysis.

claim: Further extension of 10C was efficiently inhibited by Nun.
source: However, further extension of 10C was efficiently inhibited by Nun (Figure 1B, lane 4).
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating Nun inhibits translocation.

claim: Nun alone efficiently binds the Eco TEC-9A and inhibits RNAP translocation.
source: We conclude that Nun alone efficiently binds the Eco TEC-9A and inhibits RNAP translocation, indicating that our reconstituted system captures Nun function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: TEC-20A, like TEC-9A, is active in elongation and Nun-mediated arrest.
source: TEC-20A, like TEC-9A, is active in elongation and Nun-mediated arrest (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data demonstrating TEC-20A activity.

claim: Mild glutaraldehyde crosslinking was used to stabilize the Nun/TEC complex, resulting in high Nun occupancy.
source: We used mild glutaraldehyde crosslinking to stabilize the Nun/TEC complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), resulting in high Nun occupancy.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach to improve Nun occupancy.

source: The cryoEM density maps have been deposited in the EM Data Bank with accession codes EMD-8584 (X-Nun/TEC), EMD-8585 (X-TEC), and EMD-8586 (TEC).
evidence: This is a statement about data deposition.

source: Atomic coordinates have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession codes 5UP6 (X-Nun/TEC), 5UPA (X-TEC), and 5UPC (TEC).
